title: Saddle-To-Saddle Dynamics in Deep ReLU Networks: Low-Rank Bias in the First Saddle Escape
claim: Deeper layers show stronger low-rank bias: one dominant singular value emerges after the first saddle escape and persists through training.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right; loss curve with colored vertical lines marking sampled iterations
description: Three line plots sit side by side. Panel (a), "Training Loss", plots loss against step (about 1e6 to 1.9e6). The loss drops from about 2.3 to a long plateau near 1.8, then falls to roughly zero. A red dashed vertical line marks a point on the plateau, and a blue dashed line marks the end. Panels (b) "After the first saddle escape" and (c) "Final Iteration" plot the top 10 singular values s_i(W_ℓ) against layer index ℓ from 1 to 6, one colored line per singular value. In (b), one blue top line stays near 3–4 and rises to about 6.5 at layer 6, while the other lines collapse to about 0 by layer 3. In (c), the top line reaches about 12 at layer 6, but a few other lines stay nonzero in the early layers. The eye goes first to the isolated blue line in the two right panels.
caption: Deeper layers show a stronger bias toward low-rank structure than earlier layers on MNIST. Left: Training loss over training time. Vertical lines indicate the specific iterations at which singular values are extracted. Center and Right: Top 10 singular values of the weight matrices per layer ℓfor layers 1–6 including input and output layer.
abstract: When a deep ReLU network is initialized with small weights, gradient descent (GD) is at first dominated by the saddle at the origin in parameter space. We study the so-called escape directions along which GD leaves the origin, which play a similar role as the eigenvectors of the Hessian for strict saddles. We show that the optimal escape direction features a low-rank bias in its deeper layers: the first singular value of the $\ell$-th layer weight matrix is at least $\ell^{\frac{1}{4}}$ larger than any other singular value. We also prove a number of related results about these escape directions. We suggest that deep ReLU networks exhibit saddle-to-saddle dynamics, with GD visiting a sequence of saddles with increasing bottleneck rank (Jacot, 2023).
